summary: Question: why should the Sharpe ratio not be used as the universal measure of strategy quality. Method: conceptual critique (stationarity, parametricity, perverse incentives, examples), no data. Conclusion: use Sharpe cautiously, check stationarity, prefer semi-variance and long-term return under a risk constraint.

coverage.note: definition of Sharpe, stationarity and parametricity, non-stationary track records, tail-risk strategies, footnote 1
serial correlation, symmetric deviation penalising upside, Sortino, small-consistent-profit example, solutions, references

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: it undoubtedly has some value as a measure of strategy “quality”, but it also has several crucial limitations
claims.claim: The Sharpe ratio (mean excess return over standard deviation, devised 1966 for mutual funds) has some value as a quality measure but crucial limitations.
claims.exact_rule: Sharpe = average period return in excess of the risk-free rate / standard deviation of returns

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: its widespread and often indiscriminate adoption as a quality measure is leading to distortion of proper investment priorities, as investment firms manipulate strategies and data to maximise it.
claims.claim: Indiscriminate use of Sharpe as the quality measure distorts priorities because firms manipulate strategies and data to maximise it.
claims.conditions: Incentive effect when Sharpe is the target metric

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: whilst return is a definite and meaningful quantity (an “observable”), risk is not.
claims.claim: Core objection: return is observable but risk is not; standard deviation can be computed on any series but does not mean the same thing across series.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: the return time series must be generated from a process that is both stationary and parametric.
claims.claim: Standard deviation is only a meaningful risk statistic if the return process is stationary (constant variance, skew, kurtosis) and parametric (a distribution with parameters of known meaning).
claims.exact_rule: precondition: stationary AND parametric return process

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: A common violation of this in track records occurs when a manager’s style or leverage changes over the course of their history.
claims.claim: Track records are commonly non-stationary because style or leverage changes, early records on small assets (exploiting anomalies, 'swinging for the bleachers') differ from later ones, and growing AUM forces strategy change.
claims.conditions: Small-AUM early record vs large-AUM later record

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: A simple test of rolling standard deviation through time (or even average period change) may be sufficient to uncover the manifestations of the resulting non-stationarity.
claims.claim: Proposed check: rolling standard deviation (or rolling average period change) through time reveals non-stationarity.
claims.exact_rule: compute rolling standard deviation and rolling mean of period changes over the track record; look for drift

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: It is probably too demanding to ask that a manager’s record show no style drift at all; markets are dynamic things and some change over time is unavoidable.
claims.claim: Zero style drift is too demanding; the standard is reasonable stationarity before computing statistics.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: In a non-parameterisable distribution, it conveys no information about anything. Non-stationary distributions are non-parameterisable.
claims.claim: Non-stationary distributions are non-parameterisable, so standard deviation conveys no information; Cauchy-Paretian distributions have infinite variance and would not be assessed well by Sharpe.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: some will produce many small profits and the occasional large loss - before the loss has appeared such strategies will have a high Sharpe ratio!
claims.claim: Strategies with many small gains and rare large losses (short-volatility style, merger arbitrage, LTCM) look excellent on Sharpe until the loss arrives; footnote 1 cites Goetzmann et al. 2002 on option-like strategies engineering high Sharpe without skill.
claims.conditions: Before the tail loss appears; short-sample track records

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: while the serial correlation of monthly returns common in the more illiquid hedge fund strategies (e.g. convertible arbitrage) can lead to a substantial overstatement of Sharpe ratios (Asness et al. 2001; Lo 2001).
claims.claim: Serial correlation in monthly returns of illiquid strategies (e.g. convertible arbitrage) substantially overstates Sharpe ratios (Asness, Krail, Liew 2001; Lo 2001).
claims.testable: yes - cited; computable by autocorrelation adjustment

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Some trading approaches which are swift to take profit but run losses may also twist the statistics to their advantage
claims.claim: Strategies that take profits quickly and let losses run (negative skew) flatter Sharpe.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: large positive returns increase the perception of risk as though they could as easily be negative, which for a dynamic investment strategy may not be the case.
claims.claim: Standard deviation penalises large positive returns, so removing a strategy's best returns can raise its Sharpe ratio, which Harding calls a reductio ad absurdum, and which matters for positively skewed (trend-like) dynamic strategies.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: We might suggest an improvement by considering only the negative semi-standard deviation for the denominator, a measure known as the Sortino ratio.
claims.claim: Replacing standard deviation by negative semi-standard deviation (Sortino) is a partial fix, still requiring stationarity and parametricity.
claims.exact_rule: Sortino-type ratio: excess return / downside (negative) semi-standard deviation
claims.conditions: Semi-deviation must come from a well-understood stationary distribution

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: a string of very small but consistent profits which will produce a very high Sharpe ratio with very little return.
claims.claim: Very small but consistent profits (e.g. AAA commercial paper slightly above risk-free) give a very high Sharpe with little return and say nothing about skill; this may not be caught by other tests even in a long sample.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Who would prefer to make 0.01% over risk-free each month rather than 1% with a standard deviation of 1%?
claims.claim: Illustration: 0.01% per month over risk-free would have a far higher Sharpe than 1% with 1% standard deviation, yet few would prefer it, so raw return still matters.
claims.reported_result: Hypothetical: 1% monthly return with 1% sd (monthly Sharpe 1.0) vs 0.01% per month over risk-free (no sd given); no empirical numbers

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: They are all mirrored in the (faulty) decision-making processes of investors who overvalue short run consistent returns and biased return-generating processes.
claims.claim: Author asserts the Sharpe distortions are practical, reflected in investors overvaluing short-run consistent returns and biased return-generating processes.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Suggested solutions include paying more attention to stationarity and parametricity in making estimates of future return and risk from manager track records;
claims.claim: Recommended remedies: check stationarity and parametricity, use flexibly designed quality statistics, prefer semi-variance to variance as the risk measure, and revive long-term return subject to a risk constraint as the quality statistic.
claims.exact_rule: evaluate strategies by long-term return subject to a risk constraint; use semi-variance; test stationarity/parametricity
claims.conditions: No numeric thresholds or backtests given
